title: Shakti as a philosophy
hook: a dancer finishes her performance, sees she has been fully seen, and leaves the stage

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakti as a philosophy in the Gita: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and the sense of I, all one nature, and a higher one holding the world up. Did you catch your racing mind and call it nature? Day one thousand eighty-six.
screen: `ALL OF THIS IS MINE, AND THERE IS MORE.`

segments.voice: A dancer steps onto a stage. She moves, turns, tells a whole story with her hands and eyes. The audience watches. And at some point the dance is complete: everything she came to show has been shown. So she stops, and walks off. That small scene is a picture from Samkhya, one of the philosophical schools of India, in a short book of verses called the Samkhya Karika. Samkhya isn't a hymn to a goddess. It's a cool, careful map of the world. But its picture of nature as a performer is worth holding right next to Shakti. Today: the dancer, and who she's dancing for.
screen: `A DANCER, A STAGE, AN AUDIENCE.` → `EVERYTHING SHOWN, SHE STOPS.` → `WHO IS SHE DANCING FOR?`

segments.voice: Samkhya names two principles. Purusha: pure awareness, the one who watches. Prakriti: nature, everything that moves and changes, including body and mind. Here is the verse, in paraphrase: as a dancer stops dancing after showing herself to the audience, so prakriti stops after showing herself to purusha. First, look at who does the moving. Awareness, in this picture, doesn't dance. It just sees. All the motion, the whole show of the world, belongs to nature. That's very close to what this week has heard: Shiva still, Shakti moving. Second, why she dances. The Samkhya Karika says nature works for the sake of awareness, so that it can be seen, and so that the watcher can be free. Another verse gives a homelier picture: the two together are like a lame man and a blind man. One can see but can't walk; the other can walk but can't see. Together they get somewhere. Third, the most tender line. The text says there is nothing more modest than prakriti: once she knows she has been seen, she does not show herself again. Fourth, the difference. In Samkhya, prakriti is not a goddess and is not worshipped. It's a principle in a system. Some goddess traditions take the picture and change its weight. In their reading the dancer is no lower than the watcher; she is the divine power itself, and some go further and say she is the watcher too. Samkhya and the goddess texts read the same stage differently, and both readings are part of Hindu thought. What the dancer gives everyone is a way to see motion: not as noise, but as a performance meant to be seen.
screen: `PURUSHA WATCHES. PRAKRITI MOVES.` · `SHE DANCES SO THE WATCHER CAN BE FREE.` · `NOTHING MORE MODEST THAN PRAKRITI.` · `A PRINCIPLE HERE, A GODDESS THERE.` · then, large: `SHOWN, SEEN, AND FREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the dance. Sit still, and let the breath move on its own. Let yourself be the audience. Thoughts will come onstage: a plan, a worry, a song. Sounds will come: a car, a bird, the hum of a fridge. Feelings will come: a twinge, an itch, a warm patch of sun. Don't chase any of them off. Watch each one the way you'd watch a dancer, with interest, until it has finished showing itself and leaves. If you pray, you can rest in the name you use for the divine. If you don't, rest in the watching. The bell holds the time.
Shakti as a philosophy. In Samkhya, prakriti dances for purusha, the watcher, and when she has been fully seen, she stops.
Your line: Shakti as a philosophy. Today, when a strong feeling arrives, watch it like a dancer: let it show itself fully, and see if it walks off on its own. Day one thousand eighty-six.

howItsDone: The Samkhya Karika is studied in courses on Indian philosophy and in yoga schools, where its two principles, purusha and prakriti, are used to explain the Yoga Sutras.

original.note: Sanskrit: purusha, in Samkhya the pure awareness that watches nature's dance.

what it means: in Samkhya, nature performs so awareness can see it and be free, and then she stops.

notes: Samkhya Karika paraphrased: 21 (paṅgvandhavat, the lame and the blind), 56–57 (nature acts for the sake of purusha's freedom), 59 (the dancer), 61 (nothing more modest/delicate than prakriti, sukumārataraṃ … yā dṛṣṭāsmīti punar na darśanam upaiti). Confirm verse numbers and the 'modest' rendering.
'one of the best-remembered pictures in Samkhya' is a soft superlative; editor may cut to 'a picture in Samkhya'.
Author Ishvarakrishna deliberately not named, to avoid a date/author claim.
